title: Raining Tables
text:
🌧️ Raining Tables 🌧️
Hey, analyst! Welcome to 🌧️ Raining Tables 🌧️, a precipitation- and plumbing-themed package that puddle-jumps through a minimal data pipeline.
In this package, we’re hooking up a daily precipitation table so live data can flow through NOAA’s public API to our environment and out to databases and dashboards. We’ll:

read in a spreadsheet,
explore various ways to output it (csv, Excel, PDF),
pull data updates from NOAA’s API (thanks, NOAA!),
read out to a database,
weatherproof with basic testing and maintenance,
save our outputs to Google Drive,
create a simple dashboard,
put all our code in a container, and
run it from ☁️ the cloud. ☁️

By walking through these steps, this package aims to help you understand your script as part of an automated analytical pipeline, one that might flow from:
Public data APIs > Report templates > Databases
                                    > APIs > Dashboards
                                    > Excel/PDFs/other outputs > Google Drive
                                    > Containers > Cloud


Credits & Disclaimers
🌧️ Raining Tables 🌧️ is not intended to teach you to code. A variety of teaching tools are available for learning to code. Code syntax is unlikely to be your bottleneck these days, particularly with the advent of Claude Code and other AI tools.
Views my own and do not reflect the views of any current or prior employer. I receive no compensation for this blog or any recommended resources on it.
🌧️ Raining Tables 🌧️ Data Credits:
Daily summaries from NOAA’s National Centers for Environmental Information’s Global Historical Climatology Network. You all are awesome ❤️ Weather data is critical infrastructure.
Formal data citation:

title: 1  Static output drip

Read in the raw data
Hey analyst! Welcome to Chapter 1 of 🌧️ Raining Tables 🌧️
Today, we’re taking the first small step using static files: read in precipitation.csv from data-raw/, plot it in a nice chart, and export it as a table. As static files, these outputs are friendly and easily shareable.
This may already be a very familiar process for you, and if so, excellent! All other chapters incrementally replace pieces of this chapter.
Let’s read in our static csv, data-raw/precipitation.csv.
# reading in our NOAA spreadsheet
rainfall_raw <- readr::read_csv("data-raw/precipitation.csv")

title: 1  Static output drip
text:
Now, to our static outputs! ⚡
Today, we’re outputting a simple chart and table, outputs you’d likely circulate once you received data updates. Fortunately, the Quarto format can handle both!
The Quarto format’s quite flexible. We can:


Run code in multiple languages. We’re currently running R code, but Quarto can also run Python, Julia, and Observable.


Output to multiple file types. The standard format is html, but you can also output to Word, PDF, slides, and other file formats.

Quarto report workflows:


Artwork from “Hello, Quarto” keynote by Julia Lowndes and Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel, presented at RStudio Conference 2022. Illustrated by Allison Horst.

Plotting raindrops 🫧
First, we’ll plot precipitation. If a dataset is new-to-us, plots help us explore and learn about it. If we’re already familiar, plots help us identify and follow trends.
The plot code lives in R/plot_rainfall.R rather than here in the chapter. Take a look! Having a separate, standalone function will let us format and output it automatically in Chapter 10.

rainfall_plot <- plot_rainfall(rainfall)
rainfall_plot






Figure 1.1: Daily precipitation




Then we save out the plot as a .png in outputs/rainfall_chart_01.png:

ggplot2::ggsave(
  filename = "outputs/rainfall_chart_01.png",
  plot = rainfall_plot,
  width = 8,
  height = 5
)

Exporting static files
Once we update, we often have to get our data out to a wider audience, who may only be interested in static files, like .csvs, PDFs, or Excel. We’ll also save these out to outputs/ (see R/export_outputs.R for code).
Here’s how we do that:
A csv is our universal, pipeline-friendly format, easy for another script, language, or database loader to pick up:

write_csv(
  rainfall,
  "outputs/raintable_01.csv"
)

Excel is for handoffs to stakeholders who prefer handling Excel files. Since Excel has a more complex format, we’re using the openxlsx package to read out to Excel, rather than a non-proprietary csv file format.
While they’re common outputs, Excel files are uncommon in data pipelines. Multiple sheets, too much styling, embedded formulas all make this format less usable than a simple csv.

openxlsx::write.xlsx(
  rainfall,
  "outputs/raintable_01.xlsx",
  sheetName = "raintable_01"
)

A gt table as a PDF gives you a static PDF report, good for presentations and attachments.
PDFs are also common outputs, but you wouldn’t use them in a data pipeline unless your files were handed to you this way and/or you had no other choice. They were never designed to be machine-readable; it’s easy to misread or misinterpret PDF information.







ImportantCheckpoint



Before moving on, check that outputs/ now contains four files: rainfall_chart_01.png, raintable_01.csv, raintable_01.xlsx, and raintable_01.pdf. If any are missing, sec-troubleshooting has the usual suspects.

title: 1  Static output drip
text:
Static output recap
Starting from a csv sitting in data-raw/, we tidied up its field names, plotted daily precipitation, and exported the results into outputs/.
A big downside: how much work our static drip is to update. Our rain data updates daily, but with our current static data source, we’ll have to redownload and rerun every day.
Next up: rather than read in static files, we’ll pull our rain data directly from NOAA’s API. ⚡

title: 2  Public APIs: Our Water Main
text:
API Calls
Hey analyst! Welcome to Chapter 2 of 🌧️ Raining Tables 🌧️
Hold onto your hats! 🪁 Today, we’re talking about APIs. ⛲
Today we’re hooking up to our NOAA API water main. No more hauling csvs around; we’ll have our data on tap. 🚰
Said differently: instead of re-downloading a csv every update, running our scripts will call NOAA’s API directly and pull their data into our programming environment.
✨ ~ pretty amazing ~ ✨
So how do APIs work?
First, we need to request an API key🔑 , a user password we add to our API call so NOAA recognizes us, like our ID:
Format your .Renviron file as:
NOAA_CDO_KEY=abcde12345
where NOAA_CDO_KEY is an example name you make up for your key and abcde12345 is the API key 🔑 you received from NOAA.
No spaces, no quotes.
Have your API key safely saved in .Renviron? Excellent, let’s start! 🥳
Most API calls are a URL that combine your unique API key 🔑 with a collection of other strings, data parameters that identify our specific data cut. These parameters might specify a particular date range, series ID, time frequency, unit of measurement, data flags, or other attributes.
Knowing how to format the call requires reading the data source materials and reviewing their examples. The format’s quite fiddly! If we don’t string the parameters together in the exact order, the API call won’t go through.
Let’s walk through the NOAA call from R/pull_daily_rain. Remember we’re hooking up to our data source water main ⛲: we’ll explore the different pipes, then connect the pipes together and test our taps. 🚰

title: 2  Public APIs: Our Water Main
text:
Our API key
For calling data in a report, we first save our key as an object (api_key) and use nchar() to check it exists without printing it and exposing it:

# Sys.getenv() is how we call our key from the .Renviron environment file 🔑
api_key <- Sys.getenv("NOAA_CDO_KEY")
nchar(api_key) # returns 32 if it's set, 0 if it isn't
#> [1] 32

What we’re asking for
We may want many cuts of data, so R/pull_daily_rain API call should be relatively flexibly and easy to change. For this we set our data parameters as function arguments. Change our arguments lets us retrieve different cuts of data.
To show this concretely, let’s set the parameters for a data cut for zipcode 97205, the beautiful but rainy Portland, Oregon. 🌧️

zipcode <- "97205"
date_start <- "2024-01-01"
date_end <- "2024-12-31"
units <- "standard"
limit <- 1000

location_params <- paste0("&locationid=ZIP:", zipcode) # specifies we're using zipcodes for location
location_params
#> [1] "&locationid=ZIP:97205"

Side note: if you look in R/pull_daily_rain, you’ll see it’s our choice to use zip codes to specify location in location_params. NOAA also gives us the option to specify location using weather station IDs, IDs for the specific sites weather data are collected. Finding weather station IDs takes a bit more digging, though, so we’re using zip codes.
The URL
Next, we string our URL strings together, like fitting pipes. 🔧

# stringing our data cut parameters to NOAA's URL string:

url_string <- paste0(
  "https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/cdo-web/api/v2/data?",
  "datasetid=GHCND",
  "&datatypeid=PRCP",
  location_params,
  "&startdate=", date_start,
  "&enddate=", date_end,
  "&units=", units,
  "&limit=", limit
)

# just keep stringing 🐟

url_string
#> [1] "https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/cdo-web/api/v2/data?datasetid=GHCND&datatypeid=PRCP&locationid=ZIP:97205&startdate=2024-01-01&enddate=2024-12-31&units=standard&limit=1000"

URL formats
Note: the NOAA API’s standard URL string typically won’t change unless NOAA intentionally updates its backend infrastructure. If we’re building a product using NOAA’s API, we should subscribe to NOAA updates or notifications so they can communicate any changes to us.
Reliable public data flows and user communications are hallmarks of working #publicdatainfrastructure. ⛲ 🌉 ⛲ 🚃 ⛲ 🌆
We’ve added all the parameters we need for our data cut! Last step: including your API key. 🔑






ImportantWhere the key goes



In the case of the NOAA API, we’re not adding our API key 🔑 directly into our call URL. NOAA wants it in a request header, which is a bit different (see code below).
Many other APIs expect &api_key=... directly added to url_string. If that’s the case, the full URL itself is a secret: don’t print it, don’t log it, don’t paste it anywhere. 🤫 For other APIs, review their user manual and check their API call format.


Calling our data

response <- httr::RETRY(
  verb = "GET",
  url = url_string,
  httr::add_headers(token = api_key),
  httr::timeout(10),
  times = 3,
  pause_base = 1,
  pause_cap = 10,
  quiet = TRUE
)

response
#> Response [https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/cdo-web/api/v2/data?datasetid=GHCND&datatypeid=PRCP&locationid=ZIP:97205&startdate=2024-01-01&enddate=2024-12-31&units=standard&limit=1000]
#>   Date: 2026-09-29 23:40
#>   Status: 200
#>   Content-Type: application/json
#>   Size: 41.5 kB

RETRY() is GET() with a fail-safe built in:

if the first call doesn’t go through, or if the connection times out, it waits and tries again instead of failing.


pause_base = 1 and pause_cap = 10 create this recurring call for us.

If we need it, the response output above also contains information about our call status (ie, if it ran successfully) and any associated messages. If our call fails, we can check error or other messages by viewing its status:

httr::status_code(response)
#> [1] 200
httr::http_status(response)
#> $category
#> [1] "Success"
#> 
#> $reason
#> [1] "OK"
#> 
#> $message
#> [1] "Success: (200) OK"







TipSeeing the HTTP request in action



As an experiment, let’s see our call in action by wrapping it in httr::with_verbose():

httr::with_verbose(
  httr::GET(url_string, httr::add_headers(token = "put-a-fake-token-here"))
)

The console output shows us step-by-step what we’re doing when we send this call: our request, a request timestamp, where the data are hosted, the content size and type, and whether the call ran successfully:
-> shows what we sent. <- shows what’s returned.
Why use a fake token? The verbose output prints your headers, including your API key🔑. Remember, if you run it with your real key, you’ll reveal the key in your console history or log. This is also why “here’s my verbose output” is a common way to leak a key. Watch where you put your keys! 🤫


What’s returned

parsed <- httr::content(response, as = "parsed", type = "application/json")

# as we see, our data are returned with values nested in a named list
str(parsed, max.level = 2)

#>  $ metadata:List of 1

Most APIs return data in a format called JSON as a list of nested values. There are two top-level pieces: metadata, which describes the response, and results, our data.
Under parsed$metadata, we can review parsed$metadata$resultset to ensure we’ve collected all the data we asked for, rather than hitting NOAA’s data limit:

parsed$metadata$resultset
#> $offset
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $count
#> [1] 359
#> 
#> $limit
#> [1] 1000







Warningcount vs. limit



count shows how many observations NOAA returned from our request, but limit is its observation cap. If count is larger than limit, we didn’t get all our data, just the first page, with no error to warn us.
NOAA’s ceiling is 1000 observations per request, and a year of daily precipitation data for a given zip code can blow past that. The fix is the offset parameter: ask again starting at record 1001, then 2001, until you’ve got count of them.


Unnesting our table
Finally, let’s look at our data. Here’s first row of observations in our data, stored as a list of five fields: date, datatype, station, attributes, value.

str(parsed$results[1])
#> List of 1
#>  $ :List of 5
#>   ..$ date      : chr "2024-01-01T00:00:00"
#>   ..$ datatype  : chr "PRCP"
#>   ..$ station   : chr "GHCND:USC00356749"
#>   ..$ attributes: chr ",,7,2200"
#>   ..$ value     : num 0

In parsed$results, we have hundreds of observations stored the same way. They’re nested and inconvenient to access like this, though. Let’s convert this list to a dataframe.

rain <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(parsed$results, as.data.frame))

# the first five rows in our dataframe in a simple table

lapply(..., as.data.frame) turns each one-observation list into a one-row data frame, and bind_rows() stacks them together.
What if your API call fails?
It’s pretty common for API calls to fail on the first try, especially if you’re requesting a large amount of data or if your connection’s spotty. We can usually resolve this by trying multiple times, like in httr::RETRY(). If your call’s still failing or simply taking a long time, and you’re sure it’s not a bug, consider breaking up your data request into smaller cuts. For example, if you’re having trouble pulling ten years of data, try two calls pulling five years of data.
If at first you don’t succeed, try, try again! 😆
More importantly, how do we know if our call fails? Unless our program flags the fail, it’ll continue running, try to parse the error message, and error out. To prevent this from happening, we need to add checks:

# us calling an API with a nonexistent key
bad <- httr::GET(url_string, httr::add_headers(token = "definitely-not-a-token"))

httr::status_code(bad)
#> [1] 400
httr::stop_for_status(bad, task = "pull data from NOAA CDO API")
#> Error:
#> ! Bad Request (HTTP 400). Failed to pull data from NOAA CDO API.

Despite the bad call, GET() doesn’t throw any errors. 🧐 Counterintuitively, GET() has no reason to flag failed calls unless we tell it to. stop_for_status() is our flag. Without it, our script sails on 🌊 ⛵ 🏔️, tries to parse an error message as data 💥 🏔️, and stalls out. If we don’t add this kind of check, we’ll be wondering why our run failed and have to debug.
The whole function
Everything above, with the printing taken out and the edge cases put in:


Code
R/pull_daily_rain.R

#' Pull daily rain
#'
#' Pull daily precipitation data from the NOAA Climate Data Online (CDO) Web Services API, either
#' for a zip code (using NOAA's own zip-to-station aggregation) or for one
#' or more specific stations (e.g. the output of \code{find_nearby_stations()}).
#'
#' Dependencies: httr, dplyr
#'
#' Request a NOAA CDO Web Services API key here:
#' https://www.ncdc.noaa.gov/cdo-web/token
#'
#' NOAA's API documentation can be found here:
#' https://www.ncdc.noaa.gov/cdo-web/webservices/v2
#'
#' You can search NOAA's data resources using their CDO Search here:
#' https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/cdo-web/search
#'
#' A good explainer of how to search NOAA weather data:
#' https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YY8JYbEO3Ow
#'
#' @param api_key Character. Your NOAA CDO API key.
#' @param zipcode Character. 5-digit US zip code (keep as character to
#'   preserve leading zeros, e.g. "02138"). Ignored if \code{stationid} is
#'   supplied.
#' @param stationid Character vector, optional. One or more NOAA station IDs
#'   (e.g. "GHCND:US1WAKG0072"), such as the \code{id} column returned by
#'   \code{find_nearby_stations()}. When supplied, data is pulled for these
#'   specific stations instead of the zip code's default station pool.
#' @param date_start Character. Start date, format "YYYY-MM-DD".
#' @param date_end Character. End date, format "YYYY-MM-DD". NOAA CDO API
#'   requires date ranges of one year or less per request for GHCND.
#' @param units Character. "standard" or "metric". Defaults to "standard".
#' @param limit Integer. Max records per request (NOAA's ceiling is 1000).
#'   Defaults to 1000.
#'
#' @return A data frame of daily precipitation (PRCP) records, or an empty
#'   data frame with a warning if no data is returned.
#'
#' @importFrom httr RETRY add_headers stop_for_status content timeout
#' @importFrom dplyr bind_rows
#'
#' @export
pull_daily_rain <- function(
    api_key,
    zipcode = NULL,
    stationid = NULL,
    date_start,
    date_end,
    units = "standard",
    limit = 1000,
    timeout_sec = 10,
    retry_times = 3
) {
    if (is.null(zipcode) && is.null(stationid)) {
        stop("Supply either zipcode or stationid.")
    }

    if (!is.null(stationid)) {
        # one or more stations: repeat stationid= for each, per NOAA's API
        location_params <- paste0("&stationid=", stationid, collapse = "")
    } else {
        zipcode <- as.character(zipcode) # guard against leading-zero loss
        location_params <- paste0("&locationid=ZIP:", zipcode)
    }

    ## ---- url-string

    url_string <- paste0(
        "https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/cdo-web/api/v2/data?",
        "datasetid=GHCND",
        "&datatypeid=PRCP",
        location_params,
        "&startdate=",
        date_start,
        "&enddate=",
        date_end,
        "&units=",
        units,
        "&limit=",
        limit
    )

    ## ---- api-call

    response <- tryCatch(
        httr::RETRY(
            verb = "GET",
            url = url_string,
            httr::add_headers(token = api_key),
            httr::timeout(timeout_sec),
            times = retry_times,
            pause_base = 1,
            pause_cap = 10,
            quiet = TRUE
        ),
        error = function(e) {
            stop(
                "Failed to reach NOAA CDO API after ",
                retry_times,
                " attempts -- ",
                "check your internet connection or try increasing timeout_sec. ",
                "Original error: ",
                conditionMessage(e),
                call. = FALSE
            )
        }
    )

    httr::stop_for_status(response, task = "pull data from NOAA CDO API")

    ## ---- convert-json

    parsed <- httr::content(response, as = "parsed", type = "application/json")

    if (length(parsed$results) == 0) {
        warning("No precipitation data returned for this request.")
        return(data.frame())
    }

    dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(parsed$results, as.data.frame))
}

text:
Mind Your Metadata
In rainingtables, we’re pulling data from the NOAA Global Historical Climatology Network Daily (GHCNd). Let’s take a look and review NOAA’s notes on these data to understand what we’re working with.
As NOAA explains, the GHCNd is an integrated database of daily climate summaries from more than 100,000 weather stations across 180 countries and territories worldwide. In addition to data on total precipitation, summaries provide minimum and maximum temperature, snowfall, and snow depth.
Weather stations vary in (a) how many fields and observations they provide and (b) how long they’ve been operational:
We can see this in action:
With clean, accessible, and detailed data like NOAA’s, you may be tempted to jump into analysis and overlook key metadata and data exploration. Resist! Some metadata fields contain user notes from our nice NOAA nerds. They want you to know what you’re looking at.
🌂
As an example, let’s pick iconic places in a few rainy cities to pull data from:
Let’s use their zipcodes to pull their precipitation data and walk through it.
# pull data for these zipcodes
zipcodes <- c("13202", "97205", "49504")

# not all zipcodes have a weather station in them
# safe_pull allows the function to continue if it returns a null result on one zipcode
safe_pull <- purrr::safely(pull_daily_rain)

# pulling data from the past three months
rain_list <- purrr::map(zipcodes, function(z) {
  safe_pull(
    api_key = Sys.getenv("NOAA_CDO_KEY"),
    zipcode = z,
    date_start = Sys.Date() - months(3),
    date_end = Sys.Date()
  )
}) |> purrr::set_names(zipcodes)

example_table <- rain_list |>
    purrr::map("result") |>
    purrr::compact() |>
    purrr::imap_dfr(function(df, zip) {
        df |>
            mutate(zipcode = zip)
    }) |>
    bind_rows()

See Column 4, attributes? These are data notes from NOAA. They help us understand what we’re seeing if we can crack the code. How can we interpret attributes? Look at the attributes values in zipcode 49504 observations. How do we find out what “N” means?
The answer: it takes a bit of fishing on NOAA’s website. 🎣
🐟 Fish 1: metadata manuals.
Most public data sources have at least one metadata manual available to help you interpret their data. NOAA’s no exception:
Okay, what is a naught check? 🧐
🐠 Fish 2: more metadata mining.
🐡 Fish 3: ask the experts! 🙋‍♀️
☂️
SELF NOTES: * RE: Grand Rapids, this is from two weather stations, and the metadata are telling you it failed checks (“N”). * Have to look up via the Climate Data Online Search to make sure you’re using current stations with good coverage. Like here: https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/cdo-web/datasets/GHCND/locations/CITY:US260009/detail#stationlist. Only three weather stateions are at 100% and are through current day.
Let’s align this with what we see in NOAA’s GHCN Documentation, which you can find reviewing their Climate Data Online Dataset Discovery page.
Their notes on daily summaries, with additional documentation here:
Since NOAA has a number of weather stations, with varying periods of observation, we can also search our city names using their Climate Data Online Search.
Let’s match this to what we can see on NOAA’s Climate Data Online Search tool.

max_rain <- rain_list |>

            mutate(date_format = as.Date(stringr::str_extract(date, ".+(?=T)"), "%Y-%m-%d")

When we look at NOAA’s Climate Data Online Dataset Discovery page, we see a link to NOAA’s GHCN Documentation.

Scroll down to page 3, and under Table 2 (Quality Flag/Attribute), we see: “N = failed naught check”.




With a bit more fishing, we find a second webpage, Global Historical Climatology Network - Daily (GHCN - Daily), Version 3. On this page, we spot a GHCNd README File, open it, and scroll down. Again we see “N = failed naught check” under QFLAG1, “the quality flag for the first day of the month.”












NoteDaily Summaries



Global Historical Climate Network includes daily land surface observations from around the world. The GHCNd was developed to meet the needs of climate analysis and monitoring studies that require data at a sub-monthly time resolution (e.g., assessments of the frequency of heavy rainfall, heat wave duration, etc.). The dataset includes observations from World Meteorological Organization, Cooperative, and CoCoRaHS networks. If observed, the station dataset includes max and minimum temperatures, total precipitation, snowfall, and depth of snow on ground. Some U.S. station data are typically delayed only 24 hours.




If we view the details of Grand Rapids, we learn NOAA has 87 weather stations in this area, but only a handful have 100% coverage through the current date.





Since we’re using a zipcode lookup
